analysis.one_liner: Strips tax breaks and mortgage backing from billion-dollar investors buying single-family homes and subsidizes affordable home construction.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late 2022 with three House supporters, the bill never received a hearing or vote and expired when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets investors whose assets top $100 million who buy houses to rent or flip. It would take away their tax deductions for mortgage interest, insurance, and depreciation on single-family homes; charge them a tax equal to the full price of any house they sell; and cut them off from mortgage backing by Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae. It also creates a tax credit to subsidize building or fixing up homes in lower-income neighborhoods for sale to ordinary buyers.
analysis.who_benefits: Families trying to buy a home who have been bidding against large investors, and moderate-income buyers in lower-income neighborhoods who would benefit from newly built or rehabilitated homes sold at prices tied to local incomes.

how_it_helps.text: Denies investors with more than $100 million in assets the tax deductions for mortgage interest, insurance, and depreciation on single-family homes (1 to 4 units), removing subsidies that favor big owners over family buyers.
Imposes an excise tax equal to the full sale price on any sale or transfer of a single-family home by such an investor, effectively eliminating the resale profit that drives bulk home buying.

Prohibits Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae from buying, lending on, guaranteeing, or securitizing mortgages made to these large investors, ending federal backing of investor mortgage borrowing.

Creates a Neighborhood Homes Credit that subsidizes construction or substantial rehabilitation of homes in lower-income census tracts for sale to buyers with family incomes at or below 140% of the local median.

analysis.who_pays: Large investors, private equity firms, and corporate landlords that own or finance single-family rentals, plus the federal Treasury, which would forgo revenue to fund the new home construction credit.

drawbacks.text: The excise tax is set at 100% of the sale price, an unusually blunt design that effectively bars large investors from ever selling a home, which could freeze investor-owned houses in place rather than push them onto the market for families.

The deduction ban and excise tax both exempt homes the investor newly built or substantially rehabilitated, so the largest investors could keep buying newly constructed homes even as existing-home purchases are penalized.

The rules only reach investors with assets above $100 million, leaving smaller but still large landlords untouched, and critics of this approach argue that limited housing supply, not institutional buying, is the bigger driver of high prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core restrictions are well aimed at a specific, easy-to-define problem: taxpayer-backed mortgage support and tax deductions flowing to billion-dollar investors competing with families for existing homes. The 100%-of-price excise tax is cruder than necessary and could have been calibrated to be punitive without being absolute, and the carve-out for new construction leaves a door open. The construction credit is a real but complex add-on whose cost to the Treasury is not small.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced; neither ever scheduled a hearing or vote, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on October 28, 2022, joined by Reps. Katie Porter and Mark Takano as the bill's only cosponsors.
It was referred that same day to the Ways and Means Committee and the Financial Services Committee, which split jurisdiction over its tax and mortgage-finance provisions.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the Congress expired on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large investors and corporate landlords in single-family rentals are better off, because they keep their tax deductions, their access to federal mortgage backing, and their freedom to keep buying homes. Aspiring homebuyers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporate landlords and their mortgage lenders

against.what_they_did: His committee, which held jurisdiction over the bill's tax provisions, took no recorded action after the referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Her committee, which held jurisdiction over the mortgage-finance provisions, took no recorded action after the referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's entire support was three House Democrats, and no Republican sponsorship is recorded.

industries.industry: Institutional single-family landlords (private equity firms, hedge funds, and rental REITs)
industries.note: The bill removes their tax deductions, imposes a 100%-of-price tax on reselling any home, and cuts off Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae financing. These investors profit by outbidding families for existing homes and renting them back to them, so their loss in this bill tracks the public's gain.

New construction and substantial rehabilitation are exempt from the investor penalties, and the Neighborhood Homes Credit subsidizes building or fixing up homes for sale to moderate-income buyers, creating a new paid pipeline for developers serving lower-income neighborhoods.

Lenders serving large investor buyers would lose a borrower class, and investors in Ginnie Mae and enterprise securities would see those pools shrink, but the restriction aims federal mortgage support at owner-occupants rather than landlords.
